# On the pointwise convergence of the number of abelian varieties over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with fixed trace

**Authors:** Zhao Yu Ma and Jit Wu Yap Address: Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA Email address: zm5336@princeton.edu Address: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA Email address: jitwuyap@mit.edu

## Abstract

Extending Katz–Sarnak heuristics, Ballini–Lombardo–Verzobio [4] conjectures a limiting distribution as $p\to\infty$ for $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)$ , the number of $g$ -dimensional PPAVs over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with trace $t$ , as a product of natural local factors $v_{l}(t)$ for non-archimedean places $l$ and the Sato-Tate measure $\operatorname{ST}_{g}$ corresponding to $\infty$ . We prove that their conjecture is true for all $g$ , i.e.

As a consequence, we obtain analogous results on the distribution of curves of genus $2$ and $3$ , answering questions of Bergström–Howe–García–Ritzenthaler [5] and [4].

## 1. Introduction

Let $C$ be a genus $g\geq 2$ curve over the prime field $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . As $C$ varies over the family of genus $g$ curves, Katz–Sarnak [20] proved a limiting law for the distribution of $\#C(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ as $p\to\infty$ . More precisely, let $\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ be the set of genus $g$ curves over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , where we count curves in $\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ with weight $\frac{1}{\#\Aut_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(C)}$ . Let $t_{p}(C)=\#C(\mathbb{F}_{p})-(p+1)$ be the trace of a curve and let its normalization be $x_{p}(C)=t_{p}(C)/\sqrt{p}$ . By the Hasse–Weil bound, we have $|x_{p}(C)|\leq 2g$ . Let $\mu_{\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}$ be the probability distribution of $x_{p}(C)$ for a randomly chosen $C\in\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ .

#### Theorem 1.1 (Katz-Sarnak for $\mathcal{M}_{g}$ [20, Theorem 10.7.12, 10.8.2]).

Let $g\geq 2$ be an integer and let $\operatorname{USp}_{2g}=\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{C})\cap U(2g)$ . Let the trace map $\tr\colon\operatorname{USp}_{2g}\rightarrow[-2g,2g]$ send a matrix in the unitary symplectic group to its trace. Define the Sato-Tate measure $\mu_{\operatorname{ST}_{g}}=\tr_{*}\mu_{\operatorname{USp}_{2g}}$ to be the pushforward of the Haar measure on $\operatorname{USp}_{2g}$ along the trace map. Then,

$$ \mu_{\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\xlongrightarrow{d}\mu_{\operatorname{ST}_{g}} $$

converges in distribution as $p\rightarrow\infty$ .

The integer $t_{p}(C)$ is the trace of the Frobenius action on the first etale cohomology group $H^{1}_{{\operatorname{et}}}(C_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}},\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ for any $l\not=p$ . Due to the Weil pairing, the Frobenius acts by a matrix $M\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ with multiplier $p$ . The underlying heuristic is then that $M$ should be randomly distributed according to the Haar measure. The closely related Sato-Tate problem, where we instead fix $C$ and vary $p$ , has very similar heuristics and one can refer to [38] for more details.

There is an analogous theorem for $\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ , the set of $g$ -dimensional principally polarized abelian varieties (PPAVs) over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with trace $t$ , where we again count with weight $\frac{1}{\#\Aut_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(A)}$ . Define the normalized trace $x_{p}(A)=t_{p}(A)/\sqrt{p}$ where $t_{p}(A)$ is the trace of the Frobenius acting on $A$ and let $\mu_{\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}$ be the distribution of $x_{p}(A)$ for a randomly chosen $A\in\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ .

#### Theorem 1.2 (Katz-Sarnak for $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ [20, Theorem 11.3.10]).

Let $g\geq 1$ be an integer. Then,

$$ \mu_{\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\xlongrightarrow{d}\mu_{\operatorname{ST}_{g}} $$

converges in distribution as $p\rightarrow\infty$ .

Recently, there has been interest [5, 4] in going beyond Katz–Sarnak to predict the pointwise behavior of the distribution $\mu_{\mathcal{M}_{g}}(t/\sqrt{p})$ and $\mu_{\mathcal{A}_{g}}(t/\sqrt{p})$ where $t$ is an integer. In other words, we want to know the weighted cardinality of $\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)$ and $\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)$ , which we define to be the set of genus $g$ curves and $g$ -dimensional PPAVs with trace exactly equal to $t$ . We take this as the central motivating question of our paper.

In [5], Bergström-Howe-Lorenzo-Ritzenthaler asks whether the following is true:

#### Question 1.3 (Naïve pointwise Katz-Sarnak for $\mathcal{M}_{g}$ [5, Conjecture 5.1]).

Let $g\geq 2$ be an integer. Is it true that

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\sqrt{p}-\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\right|\rightarrow 0 $$

as $p\rightarrow\infty$ ?

This is a much stronger statement than Theorem 1.1 and appears to be beyond the usual point counting methods over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ via the Lefschetz fixed point formula. In [4], Ballini-Lombardo-Verzobio proved that the above conjecture was false for all $g\geq 2$ and gave a corrected version. The reason for this is because Question 1.3 fails to take into account the distribution of matrices on non-archimedean places.

For each prime $l$ , the analogous random matrix heuristic predict that the distribution of the trace of $C$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ should be given by the trace of a random matrix in $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ . This was proven in [4, Theorem 2.1]. As a result, if we want to predict the “ $\mathbb{Z}$ ”-distribution of the trace, we should combine the local factors over all places of $\mathbb{Q}$ . For $l\neq p$ , we have

$$ v_{l}(t)=v_{l}^{g,p}(t)\coloneqq\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\{\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\mid\tr(\gamma)=t,\text{mult}(\gamma)=p\}}{\#\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})/(l^{k}\phi(l^{k}))} $$

where we omit the dependence on $g,p$ when it is clear from context. For $l=p$ we define $v_{p}(t)=1$ , see Remark 3.5 for more details. It is important to note that the local factors we give here are different from the ones proposed in [4], which counts projections from $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ instead, and we explain this discrepancy in Remark 3.4. After accounting for these local factors, [4] conjectures that there is an $L^{1}$ convergence of $\mu_{\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}$ and $\mu_{\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}$ to the expected distribution. We state the conjectures in the case of prime fields as follows.

#### Conjecture 1.4 ( $L^{1}$ Katz-Sarnak for $\mathcal{M}_{g}$ [4, Conjecture 3.4]).

Let $g\geq 2$ be an integer. Then,

$$ \sum_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|\rightarrow 0 $$

as $p\rightarrow\infty$ .

#### Conjecture 1.5 ( $L^{1}$ Katz-Sarnak for $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ [4, Conjecture 3.7]).

Let $g\geq 2$ be an integer. Then,

$$ \sum_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|\rightarrow 0 $$

as $p\rightarrow\infty$ .

#### Remark 1.6.

We make an elementary but important observation that while $L^{1}$ convergence is weaker than pointwise convergence, it is not too far off as $L^{1}$ convergence implies pointwise convergence for almost all $t\in[-2g\sqrt{p},2g\sqrt{p}]$ . More precisely, for any $\epsilon,\delta>0$ , we have for all sufficiently large $p$ that all $t\in[-2g\sqrt{p},2g\sqrt{p}]$ with at most $\delta\sqrt{p}$ possible exceptions satisfy

$$ \left|\frac{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\sqrt{p}-\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|<\epsilon. $$

This is a simple consequence of Chebyshev’s inequality.

Our main theorem is that Conjecture 1.5 is true.

#### Theorem 1.7.

Conjecture 1.5 is true for all $g\geq 2$ . In fact, for any $\epsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \sum_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|=O_{g}\left(\log(p)^{-1+\epsilon}\right). $$

When $g=1$ , the conjecture is true due to Gekeler’s formula [16], derived from the work of [11] and the analytic class number formula. In this simple case we actually have equality between the two terms for all $t,p$ . Other historical work for counting elliptic curves over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ are [6], [26], [15].

Despite the work done in the elliptic curve case, there has been no significant progress on the case of genus $g\geq 2$ . In our paper, we deduce Conjecture 1.4 for $g=2$ and a variant for $g=3$ using Theorem 1.7 and the Torelli map.

#### Theorem 1.8 ( $L^{1}$ Katz-Sarnak for $\mathcal{M}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{3}^{sym}$ ).

Let $\mathcal{M}_{3}^{sym}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)=\frac{\mathcal{M}_{3}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)+\mathcal{M}_{3}(\mathbb{F}_{p},-t)}{2}$ be the symmetrized distribution of $\mathcal{M}_{3}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)$ . For any $\epsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \sum_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{M}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{M}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{2}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|=O\left(\log(p)^{-1+\epsilon}\right), $$

$$ \sum_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{M}_{3}^{sym}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{M}_{3}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\operatorname{ST}_{3}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|=O\left(\log(p)^{-1+\epsilon}\right). $$

Now we explain how to deduce Theorem 1.8 from Theorem 1.7. Recall that the Torelli map $\mathcal{M}_{g}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{A}_{g}$ that sends a curve to its Jacobian is injective, and that we have $\dim(\mathcal{M}_{g})=3(g-1)$ and $\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})=g(g+1)/2$ . Furthermore, the Torelli theorem tells us that

$$ \Aut(\Jac(C))\cong\begin{cases}\Aut(C)&\text{if }C\text{ is hyperelliptic}\\
\Aut(C)\times\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}&\text{otherwise}.\\
\end{cases} $$

We first discuss the $g=2$ case. By the Weil bound, the groupoid cardinalities $\#\mathcal{M}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ and $\#\mathcal{A}_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ both have size $p^{3}+O(p^{2.5})$ . Furthermore, a genus $2$ curve is generically hyperelliptic, which means that $\#\Aut(\Jac(C))=\#\Aut(C)$ . Hence, the image of the Torelli map is almost surjective, so the $L^{1}$ convergence for $\mathcal{M}_{2}$ follows from $\mathcal{A}_{2}$ . For $g=3$ , while the groupoid cardinalities $\#\mathcal{M}_{3}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ and $\#\mathcal{A}_{3}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ both have size $p^{6}+O(p^{5.5})$ , a curve of genus $3$ is generically non-hyperelliptic, so $\#\Aut(\Jac(C))=2\#\Aut(C)$ and the image of the Torelli map contains only approximately half of the points in $\mathcal{A}_{3}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ . This obstruction can be described more precisely – if $C$ is non-hyperelliptic, the quadratic twist of its Jacobian $\Jac(C)_{\chi_{2}}$ cannot be a Jacobian, and furthermore $t_{p}(\Jac(C)_{\chi_{2}})=-t_{p}(\Jac(C))$ , see [25, Appendix] for more details. This explains why we can only prove $L^{1}$ convergence for $\mathcal{M}_{3}^{sym}$ .

One may wonder whether we can use Theorem 1.7 to prove Conjecture 1.4 for general $g$ or analogous conjectures for other families such as the moduli space of hyperelliptic curves $\mathcal{H}_{g}$ . It appears that the crux to resolving this problem is to characterize the image of the Torelli map, i.e. which PPAVs are Jacobians of curves (or hyperelliptic curves), which still remains an open problem.

We also conjecture that pointwise versions of Conjecture 1.4 and Theorem 1.7 are true. Although we fall short of proving it, we believe that a refinement of our method could lead to a possible proof, at least in the case of $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ , $\mathcal{M}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{3}^{sym}$ .

#### Conjecture 1.9 (Pointwise Global Katz-Sarnak for $\mathcal{M}_{g}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ ).

For $g\geq 2$ , we have

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{M}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\sqrt{p}-\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|\rightarrow 0 $$

as $p\rightarrow\infty$ . For $g\geq 1$ , we have

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\left|\frac{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},t)}{\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\sqrt{p}-\operatorname{ST}_{g}(t/\sqrt{p})\prod_{l}v_{l}(t)\right|\rightarrow 0 $$

as $p\rightarrow\infty$ .

### 1.1. Proof overview

The methods that are usually used to prove convergence theorems like Theorem 1.1 and 1.2 are geometric in nature, but these methods are unlikely to be strong enough to prove something global like Theorem 1.7. For example, one such method relies on computing the étale cohomology of the moduli spaces which allow us to compute moments of the trace, but this method cannot distinguish curves of trace $t$ and $t+1$ . Another possible approach is to use monodromy and Deligne’s equidistribution theorem, but this only gives us convergence over each local place. Thus, we take a completely different approach. Roughly, our proof consists of two parts – first, we derive a formula for the number of PPAVs with a fixed characteristic polynomial, then, we sum this formula up over characteristic polynomials with fixed trace.

We discuss the first part of our proof. In Section 2, we parametrize the moduli space $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ in terms of the characteristic polynomials $f_{A}$ using Honda-Tate theory, and we define the region of characteristic polynomials. In Section 3, we then prove the following formula for the number of PPAVs with a corresponding generic characteristic polynomial $f_{A}$ which may be of independent interest.

#### Theorem 1.10.

Suppose that $A$ is a simple, ordinary abelian variety whose Galois group is generic, i.e. isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ . Then, there are a nonzero number of PPAVs with characteristic polynomial $f_{A}$ , and the groupoid cardinality is given by

$$ \#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},f_{A})=p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}v_{\infty}(f_{A})\prod_{l}v_{l}(f_{A}) $$

where the local factors $v_{\infty}(f_{A})$ and $v_{l}(f_{A})$ are defined in Equation (3.2) and (3.4).

Our work in Section 2 also tells us that the conditions in Theorem 1.10 are generic among all isogeny classes. As far as we know, this is first such explicit formula for characteristic polynomials, albeit only in the generic case. Other similar formulas were given in [1] and [18], however, these count PPAVs within different classes which are finer than the data of a characteristic polynomial. We also expect there to be no such simple formula in the non-generic case, although we believe it is possible to give a concrete upper bound.

The starting point for the proof of Theorem 1.10 is Kottwitz’s orbital integral formula for the number of PPAVs in a Polarized Abelian Variety (PAV) isogeny class as stated in Theorem 3.2. Then, we built on the work of [1] which rewrites this as an Euler product of rational orbital integrals as well as a global factor including the Tamagawa number in Theorem 3.3. This was a generalization of the earlier work done by [2] for the case of elliptic curves. [1] attempts to express these rational orbital integrals explicitly in terms of a ratio of matrices projected from $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ , but we found an error in this explicit expression for the ratios. Fortunately, we only require stable orbital integrals for this paper, which can be easily expressed in the ratio of explicit matrix counts, which is explained in the appendix of this paper.

Then, to move from counts in a PAV-isogeny class to an AV-isogeny class determined by characteristic polynomial, we characterize the set of PAV-isogeny classes in an AV-isogeny with Kottwitz’s invariant and show that this is well behaved in the generic case, which allows us to sum up the counts over the PAV-isogeny classes to obtain Theorem 1.10. Note that when compared to Theorem 3.3, there is no Tamagawa number in the formula, which seems to suggest that the Tamagawa number is an adjustment factor for PAV-isogeny classes, at least in the generic case.

In Section 4 and 5, we prove some technical lemmas on the local factors which are required for the rest of the proof. While the local factors $v_{\infty}(f)$ and $v_{l}(t)$ are easy to understand, $v_{l}(f)$ is much more difficult. This is because the singularities of the associated subscheme of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ cut out by characteristic polynomial $f$ are hard to understand, which leads to difficulty bounding point counts over $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ . In Section 4.3.2 we discuss conjectures and partial results on $v_{l}(f)$ , and Section 5 is dedicated to proving these partial results. Fortunately, these partial results are enough to prove our final theorem, even though they lead to more technical difficulty in the analytical arguments. We highlight that this difficulty is intrinsic to the case of $g\geq 2$ and does not exist in the elliptic curve case, essentially because $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ is much more complicated than $\operatorname{GL}_{2}$ .

Now we explain the second part of our proof. To obtain Theorem 1.7 from Theorem 1.10, we need to sum the counts $\#\mathcal{A}_{g}(\mathbb{F}_{p},f)$ over all characteristic polynomials $f$ with a fixed trace $t$ . Similar ideas of summing Euler products in the elliptic curve case were explored in [9] and [28], however, the case of $g\geq 2$ is more difficult which requires the introduction of new ideas and methods. Most notably, we tackle an arithmetic statistic question on bounding the size of a family of exceptional number fields.

In Section 4.3 we see that for all but finitely many primes $l$ , $v_{l}(f_{A})$ is a ratio of local Dedekind zeta functions ${\zeta_{K,l}(1)}/{\zeta_{K^{+},l}(1)}$ where $K\coloneqq\mathbb{Q}[x]/f_{A}(x)$ and $K^{+}$ is the totally real subfield of $K$ , and this implies the convergence of $\prod_{l}v_{l}(f_{A})$ . In order to deal with the sum of infinite Euler products, we need to approximate $\prod_{l}v_{l}(f_{A})$ with a truncated product $\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}(f_{A})$ . In the elliptic curve case, $K$ is a quadratic field, so these reduce to Dirichlet L-functions, which allows for a completely analytic proof by looking at Dirichlet characters such as in [9]. However, this does not work in the $g\geq 2$ case as we are now concerned with Dedekind zeta functions and Artin L-functions, and thus it seems likely that a purely analytic argument would be impossible. Nevertheless, by looking at prime splitting, we see that giving such a truncation of the infinite Euler product is essentially equivalent to the statement of an effective Chebotarev theorem for the Dedekind zeta function of the Galois closure $\widetilde{K}$ . Fortunately for us, there is exactly a recent effective Chebotarev theorem in families of number fields developed by [33] and improved in [41] for general Galois group $G$ , and our problem is a natural application of this result. We state this in Theorem 6.1.

However, a key problem that arises here is the existence of exceptional fields for which the effective Chebotarev theorem could fail, and we need to bound the number of these. To do this, we use a quantitative version of Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem given in [32] which was proven using Bombieri-Pila type of methods. It is important for our application that we use a version that is only logarithmically dependent on the height of the polynomial. In more detail, we need to bound the quantity $\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{F}_{G}(Q)}$ defined in Theorem 6.1, which essentially counts the maximum number of number fields in our family that one particular number field in our family intersects. To do this, for each number field $L$ we construct a polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}[x,a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}]$ where $a_{i}$ are the variables of the characteristic polynomial $f$ , such that the irreducibility of this polynomial over $x$ given some values of $a_{1},\ldots,a_{g}$ implies that $\mathbb{Q}[x]/f(x)$ does not intersect $L$ , which allows us to apply Hilbert’s irreducibility. We discuss this in Section 6.

Finally, we finish the proof of Theorem 1.7 in Section 7 using an analytical argument which on a high level proceeds as follows. We are left with a sum of truncated products $\sum_{f}v_{\infty}(f)\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}(f)$ . We approximate $v_{l}(f)$ by an $l^{k}$ -periodic function $v_{l,k}(f)$ , so the product is $\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}l^{k}$ periodic. It would be easy to sum these products if this period is $o(p)$ by cutting the region of characteristic polynomials into boxes of $o(p)$ length. However, this is not the case. Nevertheless, we prove an averaging lemma in Section 7 which allows us to do the above, essentially by using the Taylor expansion of $\exp(\sum_{l\leq l_{0}}\log(v_{l,k}(f)))$ . Hence, by cutting the region of characteristic polynomials into boxes of size $o(p)$ , in each box $\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}(f)$ averages out to $\prod_{l\leq l_{0}}v_{l}(t)$ , and we can approximate the sum of $v_{\infty}(f)$ over these boxes with an integral, giving us the Sato-Tate distribution. Of course, the actual details are technical and complicated, notably, we need to introduce an auxiliary factor to deal with our suboptimal bounds on $v_{l}(f)$ .

## 2. Parametrization by characteristic polynomials

The rest of the paper is devoted to proving Theorem 1.7. We fix the genus $g\geq 2$ , since the $g=1$ case corresponds to elliptic curves which has already been proven in [16]. All little- $o$ or big- $O$ notation will omit the dependence on $g$ , but the dependence on all other variables like $p$ and $l$ will be included. A common theme in this paper is that we will focus on counting PPAVs in the most generic case (e.g. simple, ordinary, etc.) as this is sufficient to prove the $L^{1}$ bound we want.

### 2.1. Honda-Tate theory

This section roughly follows the exposition in [17, Section 3]. Consider an abelian variety $A$ of dimension $g$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , and its characteristic polynomial $f_{A}(x)$ which has degree $2g$ . Weil’s theorem tells us that every root of $f_{A}(x)$ is a $p$ -Weil number, i.e. an algebraic integer which has absolute value $p^{1/2}$ for every embedding into $\mathbb{C}$ . The Honda-Tate Theorem says that the map sending an abelian variety $A$ to the complex roots of $f_{A}$ induces a bijection between isogeny classes of simple abelian varieties and Galois conjugacy classes of Weil $p$ -numbers. Since every abelian variety is isogenous to a product of simple abelian varieties, this gives a partition of abelian varieties into isogeny classes, in terms of the data of $p$ -Weil numbers.

However, it is difficult to use $p$ -Weil numbers as a parametrization for counting purposes. Instead, we will use a variant of the Honda-Tate theorem for ordinary abelian varieties where isogeny classes are parametrized by characteristic polynomials. See [17, Theorem 3.3] and [40, Theorem 1].

#### Definition 2.1.

A $g$ -dimensional abelian variety $A$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ is ordinary if the set of $A[p](\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p})$ has exactly $p^{g}$ elements. A Weil $p$ -polynomial is an integer monic polynomial where all complex roots have magnitude $p^{1/2}$ . An ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial is a Weil $p$ -polynomial of even degree where $p$ doesn’t divide the middle coefficient.

#### Theorem 2.2 (Honda-Tate for ordinary abelian varieties).

The map $A\mapsto f_{A}(x)$ induces a bijection between the isogeny classes of ordinary abelian varieties of dimension $g$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ to the set of ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials of degree $2g$ . Furthermore, isogeny classes of simple ordinary abelian varieties correspond to irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials.

#### Remark 2.3.

The bijection in Theorem 2.2 does not extend to a bijection from all abelian varieties to all Weil $p$ -polynomials. Indeed, there are simple non-ordinary abelian varieties $A$ which have characteristic polynomial that is a nontrivial power of an irreducible polynomial, say $f_{A}(x)=g(x)^{r}$ . In this case, $g(x)$ is also a Weil polynomial, there is no corresponding abelian variety with characteristic polynomial $g(x)$ , as it would have to be isogenous to $A$ by the original Honda-Tate theorem.

### 2.2. The region $\mathcal{R}_{g}$

Next, we find an explicit condition on the coefficients of an ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial. Throughout the paper, we will often switch between multiplier $p$ (characteristic polynomials) and multiplier $1$ (normalized characteristic polynomials) versions of symplectic polynomials, and we will attempt to consistently denote the first kind by $f(x)$ with coefficients $a_{i}$ and the second by $g(x)$ with coefficients $b_{i}$ .

#### Definition 2.4.

Let the region $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ consist of the tuples $\mathbf{b}=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g})\in\mathbb{R}^{g}$ such that the polynomial $g_{\mathbf{b}}(x)\coloneqq x^{2g}+b_{1}x^{2g-1}+\cdots+b_{g}x^{g}+b_{g-1}x^{g-1}+\cdots+1$ has roots that come in pairs $\{e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}\}$ . Define the map $[p]:\mathbb{R}^{g}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{g}$ by sending $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g})\mapsto(b_{1}p^{1/2},\ldots,b_{g}p^{g/2})$ , i.e it scales the $i$ -th term by $p^{i/2}$ . Then, it is clear that the image $[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ contains the tuples $\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{g})\in\mathbb{R}^{g}$ such that $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)\coloneqq x^{2g}+a_{1}x^{2g-1}+\cdots+a_{g}x^{g}+pa_{g-1}x^{g-1}+\cdots+p^{g-1}a_{1}x+p^{g}$ has roots that come in pairs $\{\sqrt{p}e^{i\theta},\sqrt{p}e^{-i\theta}\}$ , because we have the relation $f_{[p](\mathbf{b})}(x)=p^{g}g_{\mathbf{b}}(x/\sqrt{p})$ .

The reason we introduced the region $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ is because it parametrizes ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials.

#### Proposition 2.5.

The ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials of degree $2g$ are exactly those of the form $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ where $\mathbf{a}\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ and $p\nmid a_{g}$ .

#### Proof.

An ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial $f(x)$ of degree $2g$ has integral coefficients, so its roots must come in pairs of $\{\sqrt{p}e^{i\theta},\sqrt{p}e^{-i\theta}\}$ or $\{-\sqrt{p},\sqrt{p}\}$ . Thus, when factored over $\mathbb{R}$ , the irreducible factors of $f(x)$ are of the form $x^{2}+tx+p$ or $x^{2}-p$ . However, it cannot have the factor $x^{2}-p$ , because otherwise we would have $f(x)=(x^{2}-p)^{r}\prod_{i=1}^{g-r}(x^{2}+t_{i}x+p)\equiv x^{2r}\prod_{i=1}^{g-r}(x^{2}+t_{i}x)=x^{r+g}\prod_{i=1}^{g-r}(x+t_{i})\pmod{p}$ for $r>0$ which clearly has middle coefficient a multiple of $p$ . It follows that an ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial must have roots that come in conjugate pairs $\{\sqrt{p}e^{i\theta},\sqrt{p}e^{-i\theta}\}$ , so it is of the form $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ with $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{g})\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ and the condition that $p\nmid a_{g}$ follows directly. The converse is clear from the definitions. ∎

We give a more abstract description of $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ which will be useful later.

#### Lemma 2.6.

Any matrix $M\in\operatorname{USp}_{2g}$ has a characteristic polynomial $g_{M}(x)$ with symmetric coefficients which can be written as $g_{\mathbf{b}}(x)$ for some $\mathbf{b}$ , so we let $\pi\colon\operatorname{USp}_{2g}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{g}$ be the map that sends $M$ to $\mathbf{b}$ . Then, $\mathcal{R}_{g}=\pi(\operatorname{USp}_{2g})$ is the image, and in particular, $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^{g}$ .

#### Proof.

Take $M\in\operatorname{USp}_{2g}\coloneqq\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{C})\cap U(2g)$ . Since $M$ is symplectic, we have $M^{-1}=\Omega^{-1}M^{T}\Omega$ where $\Omega=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&I_{g}\\ -I_{g}&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ . As eigenvalues remain the same under transposition and conjugation, $M^{-1}$ has the same eigenvalues as $M$ . Furthermore, since $M$ is also unitary, this means that eigenvalues either come in complex conjugate pairs $\{e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}\}$ or are $1$ or $-1$ . Furthermore, both $-1$ and $1$ have even multiplier because $\det(M)=1$ , and thus all roots can be grouped into complex conjugate pairs $\{e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}\}$ . It follows directly that the characteristic polynomial $g_{M}(x)$ has symmetric coefficients and that $\pi(M)\in\mathcal{R}_{g}$ . Conversely, it is clear that for any $(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g})\in\mathcal{R}_{g}$ , the corresponding polynomial is the characteristic polynomial of the diagonal matrix $\diag(e^{i\theta_{1}},\ldots,e^{i\theta_{g}},e^{-i\theta_{1}},\ldots,e^{-i\theta_{g}})\in\operatorname{USp}_{2g}$ . ∎

#### Example 2.7.

We describe the region $\mathcal{R}_{2}$ explicitly using inequalities. For $(b_{1},b_{2})\in\mathcal{R}_{2}$ , pair the conjugate roots and factorize the corresponding polynomial $x^{4}+b_{1}x^{3}+b_{2}x^{2}+b_{1}x+1=(x^{2}+tx+1)(x^{2}+sx+1)$ where $|t|,|s|\leq 2$ , so we have $b_{1}=t+s$ and $b_{2}=2+st$ . Thus, $|b_{1}|\leq 4$ , and given a fixed $b_{1}$ in this range, $b_{2}$ is maximized by taking $s=t$ and minimized when $s=2,t=b_{1}-2$ when $b_{1}\geq 0$ and $s=-2,t=b_{1}+2$ when $b_{1}\leq 0$ . Thus, $\mathcal{R}_{2}=\left\{(b_{1},b_{2})\mid|b_{1}|\leq 4,\ 2|b_{1}|-2\leq b_{2}\leq 2+(b_{1}/2)^{2}\right\}$ .

One would expect intuitively that for general $g$ that $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ can be completely described explicitly using equations, just like in the $g=2$ case. We prove a slightly weaker statement which suffices for our purposes, but before that we give a useful definition.

#### Definition 2.8.

Suppose a monic polynomial $g(x)$ of degree $2g$ has roots that come in pairs $\{e^{i\theta_{j}},e^{-i\theta_{j}}\}$ , or equivalently that it is of the form $g_{\mathbf{b}}(x)$ . Then, define the totally real polynomial $g^{+}(x)$ of degree $g$ to be the monic polynomial with roots $e^{i\theta_{j}}+e^{-i\theta_{j}}$ , so that $g(x)=x^{g}g^{+}(x+\frac{1}{x})$ . Likewise, for multiplier $p$ polynomials, if $f(x)$ has roots $\{\sqrt{p}e^{i\theta_{j}},\sqrt{p}e^{-i\theta_{j}}\}$ , define $f^{+}(x)$ to have roots $\sqrt{p}(e^{i\theta_{j}}+e^{-i\theta_{j}})$ so $f(x)=x^{g}f^{+}(x+\frac{p}{x})$ .

#### Lemma 2.9.

There exist a compact subset $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{g-1}$ and two continuous functions $s,t\colon K\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ \mathcal{R}_{g}=\{(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g})\in\mathbb{R}^{g}\mid s(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1})\leq b_{g}\leq t(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1}),(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1})\in K\}. $$

#### Proof.

We let $K$ be the projection from $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ to the first $g-1$ coordinates which is compact because Lemma 2.6 tells us that $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ is compact. Then, note that $\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{R}_{g}$ if and only if $g^{+}_{\mathbf{b}}(x)=x^{g}+c_{1}x^{g-1}+\cdots+c_{g}$ has all $g$ roots in $[-2,2]$ . By expanding the equation $g_{\mathbf{b}}(x)=x^{g}g^{+}_{\mathbf{b}}(x+\frac{1}{x})$ , it is clear that for all $0\leq i\leq g$ we have $b_{i}=c_{i}+\binom{g-i+2}{1}c_{i-2}+\binom{g-i+4}{2}c_{i-4}+\cdots$ . This system of equations is defined by a lower triangular matrix with $1$ s on the diagonal, and by inverting this matrix we get another lower triangular matrix with $1$ s on the diagonal. Thus, we can write each $c_{i}$ as $b_{i}$ plus a linear combination of $b_{i-2},b_{i-4},\ldots$ . Here, we included the variables $b_{0},c_{0}$ in our system of equations, and both are equal to $1$ .

Now, suppose we fixed $b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1}$ , which defines $c_{1},\ldots,c_{g-1}$ by the previous paragraph. Plot the graphs defined by $y=x^{g}+c_{1}x^{g-1}+\cdots+c_{g-1}x$ and the line $y=-c_{g}$ , and note that the intercepts are exactly the real roots of $g^{+}_{\mathbf{b}}(x)$ . From this we can see that all $g$ roots of $g^{+}_{\mathbf{b}}(x)$ lie in $[-2,2]$ if and only if $c_{g}$ lies in some closed (or empty) interval. By our change of variables, this happens if and on $b_{g}\in[s(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1}),t(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1})]$ for some functions $s,t$ . To prove $s$ and $t$ are continuous, note that varying $b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1}$ continuously leads to changing $c_{1},\ldots,c_{g-1}$ and the graph $y=x^{g}+c_{1}x^{g-1}+\cdots+c_{g-1}x$ continuously, which changes the interval of $c_{g}$ and hence $b_{g}$ continuously. ∎

The reason why we want $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ to be expressed in this way is that this allows us to approximate the region $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ well enough with hypercubes.

#### Proposition 2.10.

The volume $\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g})$ is well-defined and finite. Furthermore, chop up $\mathbb{R}^{g}$ into a regular grid of hypercuboids with side lengths $\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{g}\leq\epsilon$ and let $\mathcal{R}^{-}_{g}$ (resp. $\mathcal{R}^{+}_{g}$ ) be the union of the hypercuboids which are completely contained within (resp. which intersect) $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ . Then, $|\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g})-\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g}^{\pm})|=O(\epsilon)$ .

#### Proof.

This essentially follows from Lemma 2.9 and the theory of Riemann integration. We have $\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g})=\int_{K}\left(t(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1})-s(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g-1})\right)db_{1}\cdots db_{g-1}$ . To estimate this integral, consider the subdivision of $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ given in the statement, and let $\mathcal{T}$ be the set of hypercuboids intersecting $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ . Let $\pi\colon\mathbb{R}^{g}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{g-1}$ be the projection onto the first $g-1$ coordinates, so the previous subdivision induces a subdivision of $\mathbb{R}^{g-1}$ via $\pi$ , and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of hypercuboids intersecting $\mathcal{K}$ . Then, $\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g}^{+})=(\#\mathcal{T})\epsilon_{1}\cdots\epsilon_{g}=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\#\{T\in\mathcal{T}\mid\pi(T)=S\}\epsilon_{1}\cdots\epsilon_{g}$ . Since $s,t$ are continuous over a compact set, they are uniformly continuous and in particular $c$ -Lipschitz, so for each hypercuboid $S\in\mathcal{S}$ , $\left|\max(s(S))-\min(s(S))\right|<c\epsilon$ and analogously for $t$ . Hence, comparing the sum and integral over $S$ , we have $(\#\{T\in\mathcal{T}\mid\pi(T)=S\}-2)\epsilon_{1}\cdots\epsilon_{g}\leq(\min(t(S))-\max(s(S)))\epsilon_{1}\cdots\epsilon_{g-1}\leq\int_{S}t(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g})-s(b_{1},\ldots,b_{g})db_{1}\cdots db_{g}+2c\epsilon\epsilon_{1}\cdots\epsilon_{g-1}$ . Furthermore, note the cardinality of $\mathcal{S}$ is $\leq C/\epsilon_{1}\cdots\epsilon_{g}$ because $K$ is compact, so summing over $S\in\mathcal{S}$ we have $\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g}^{+})\leq\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g})+(2c+2)C\epsilon$ . The same proof works for $\mathcal{R}_{g}^{-}$ . ∎

As a corollary, we obtain the following bound on the number of ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials of degree $2g$ . Note that this has been previously proven by Dipippo and Howe [12].

#### Corollary 2.11.

There are $\Theta(p^{g(g+1)/4})$ many ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials of degree $2g$ .

#### Proof.

We chop $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ into hypercubes of side length $p^{-1/2}$ and volume $p^{-g/2}$ . In each cube, there are approximately $\frac{p-1}{p}p^{g(g-1)/4}$ tuples $(a_{1}/p^{1/2},\ldots,a_{g}/p^{g/2})$ with $p\nmid a_{g}$ . By Proposition 2.10, there are approximately $\frac{p-1}{p}\Vol(\mathcal{R}_{g})p^{g(g+1)/4}(1+O(p^{-1/2}))$ such tuples in $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ , and by Proposition 2.5 these corresponds to ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials. ∎

It is not hard to prove the same statement for all Weil $p$ -polynomials, by showing that there are $o(p^{g(g+1)/4})$ many non-ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials. A similar upper bound was derived in [27, Corollary 2.3], but a more careful analysis of the region $\mathcal{R}_{g}$ as seen in Lemma 2.9 and Proposition 2.10 was needed for our lower bound.

### 2.3. Irreducibility

We will prove that several properties are satisfied by a generic ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial, which would eventually allow us to simplify things by assuming these properties. First, we will show that a generic ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial is irreducible.

#### Lemma 2.12.

There are at most an $O(p^{-(g-1)/2})$ proportion of ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials that are reducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose an ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial can be factored over $\mathbb{Z}$ as $f(x)=r(x)s(x)$ . From the proof of Proposition 2.5, $f(x)$ and thus $r(x)$ must have roots that come in pairs $\{\sqrt{p}e^{i\theta},\sqrt{p}e^{-i\theta}\}$ . Say it is of degree $2d$ , then following the same proof we can write $r(x)=f_{\mathbf{c}}(x)$ for some $c\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{r})$ . By the proof of Corollary 2.11, there are $O(p^{d(d+1)/4})$ possibilities for $r(x)$ . Likewise, $s(x)$ has degree $2(g-d)$ and there are $O(p^{(g-d)(g-d+1)/4})$ many such $s(x)$ . We obtain the desired result by multiplying these and summing over all $d$ , noting that the worst case happens when $d$ is $1$ or $g-1$ . ∎

Recall that by Theorem 2.2 irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials correspond to simple and ordinary abelian varieties. Let $[A,\lambda]$ be a PPAV where $A$ is a simple ordinary abelian variety, and let $f_{A}$ be the characteristic polynomial which is an irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial. It is easier to describe the endomorphism ring of $A$ in this irreducible case. Let $\End^{0}(A)=\End(A)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}[\Frob_{p}]\subseteq\End^{0}(A)$ .

#### Lemma 2.13.

We have $\End^{0}(A)=K\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/f_{A}(x)$ .

#### Proof.

$\End^{0}(A)=K$ follows from [39, Theorem 2(c)], and $K\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/f_{A}(x)$ follows as $f_{A}(x)$ is irreducible, so the minimum polynomial of $\Frob_{p}$ is $f_{A}(x)$ . ∎

Note that $K$ is a CM-field, where complex conjugation sends $x\mapsto p/x$ . This action is the same as the Rosati involution on $\End^{0}(A)=K$ which is given by $\alpha\mapsto\lambda^{-1}\circ\alpha^{\vee}\circ\lambda$ . Let $K^{+}$ be the totally real subfield of $K$ fixed by complex conjugation. Then, we can write $K^{+}\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/f^{+}_{A}(x)$ where $f^{+}_{A}(x)$ is defined in Definition 2.8. Recall that $f_{A}(x)=x^{g}f_{A}^{+}(x+\frac{p}{x})$ so the irreducibility of $f_{A}(x)$ implies that of $f_{A}^{+}(x)$ .

### 2.4. Generic Galois group

We investigate the Galois group $G$ of a generic irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)=x^{2g}+a_{1}x^{2g-1}+\cdots+p^{g}$ , defined to be the Galois group of its splitting field $\widetilde{K}$ . View $G$ as a subset of $S_{2g}$ via its action on the $2g$ embeddings $\iota\colon K\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/f(x)\hookrightarrow\widetilde{K}$ sending $x$ to each of the $2g$ roots of $f(x)$ . The roots of $f(x)$ occur in conjugate pairs, so pair these embeddings accordingly as $\{\iota_{1},\iota_{2}\},\ldots,\{\iota_{2g-1},\iota_{2g}\}$ . Clearly, $G$ has to preserve these pairs, so we have $G\subseteq(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ , where the $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}$ action swaps the elements in each of the $g$ pairs and $S_{g}$ permutes the $g$ pairs. Intuitively, the generic Galois group should be as large as possible, and we will prove that this is indeed the case. Note that $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ is the Weyl group of the symplectic group.

#### Proposition 2.14.

There are at most an $O(p^{-1/4}\log p)$ proportion of irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomials which do not have Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ .

The paper [10] tackled a very similar problem, where they considered the set of reciprocal polynomials $g(x)=x^{n}g(1/x)$ with coefficients having absolute value less than $N$ , and they proved that the proportion of exceptions is at most $O(N^{-1/2}\log N)$ , essentially using a version of the large sieve. In our case, we have instead the multiplier $p$ case $f(x)=x^{2g}f(p/x)$ with the coefficients satisfying $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{g})\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ . One key difference is that in the first case $N$ is independent of the defining equation of the polynomials $g(x)=x^{n}g(1/x)$ , while in our case both the region and the defining equation depends on $p$ . Another difference is that in our case the region has side lengths with different orders of magnitude. Thus our case does not follow directly from [10]. Nevertheless, we are able to prove it by modifying their proof. Note that we change some of their variables in the following proof.

#### Proof.

Say that a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x]$ has splitting type $l$ for the prime $q$ if its factorization into irreducibles mod $q$ consists of distinct factors which are all linear except one factor of degree $l$ . For $q\neq p$ , let $\Omega_{l}(q)$ be the subset of $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{g}$ such that the corresponding $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)=x^{2g}+a_{1}x^{2g-1}+\cdots+p^{g}$ has splitting type $l$ for $q$ . Note that the proof of Lemma 3 of loc. cit. works for all $q\neq p$ because we correspondingly have $f(x)=x^{g}f^{+}(x+\frac{p}{x})$ and $p$ is a unit in $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . Thus, we have $|\Omega_{l}(q)|=0$ for odd $l$ and $|\Omega_{2k}(q)|=\frac{q^{g}}{2^{g-k+1}k(g-k)!}+O(q^{g-1})$ for $0\leq k\leq g$ . For $q=p$ , simply let $\Omega_{l}(p)$ be the empty set for all $l$ .

Let $P_{l}(x)=\sum_{q\leq x}|\Omega_{l}(q)|q^{-g}$ . For $\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{g})\in\mathbb{Z}^{g}$ , let $P_{l}(\mathbf{a},x)$ be the number of primes $q\leq x$ where $\mathbf{a}\pmod{q}$ is in $\Omega_{l}(q)$ . Lemma 5 of loc. cit. gives $\sum_{|\mathbf{a}|\leq N}(P_{l}(\mathbf{a},x)-P_{l}(x))^{2}=O(N^{g}P_{l}(x))$ for $N\geq x^{2}$ . While Lemma 5 sums over the box $[-N,N]^{g}$ , it is clear that it will also hold with any translate of $[-N,N]^{g}$ as there is nothing special about the origin. Hence, taking $N=p^{1/2}$ and $x=p^{1/4}$ , we can cover the region $[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})$ with $O(p^{g(g-1)/4})$ translates of the box to obtain $\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in[p](\mathcal{R}_{g})}(P_{l}(\mathbf{a},p^{1/4})-P_{l}(p^{1/4}))^{2}=O(p^{g(g+1)/4}P_{l}(p^{1/4}))$ .

Now let $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ be an irreducible ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial. If it has Galois group $G$ which is a proper subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ , then by Lemma 2 of loc. cit., there exists some $l\in\{2,4,2g-2,2g\}$ where $G$ doesn’t contain any $l$ -cycle. This implies that $f$ cannot have splitting type $l$ for any prime $q$ , and thus $P_{l}(\mathbf{a},p^{1/4})=0$ (see the paragraph after Lemma 4 of loc. cit.). By our first paragraph and the prime number theorem we have $P_{l}(p^{1/4})=\Theta\left(\frac{p^{1/4}}{\log p}\right)$ . Thus, by our second paragraph there can be at most $O(p^{(g^{2}+g-1)/4}\log p)$ such $f_{\mathbf{a}}(x)$ for each $l\in\{2,4,2g-2,2g\}$ . Summing up across these four $l$ s and dividing by $\Theta(p^{g(g+1)/4})$ as in Corollary 2.11 yields the result. ∎

We remark that [3] gives better quantitative bounds than [10], although their proof is more complicated and hence more difficult to adapt to our situation.

### 2.5. Existence of PPAVs

Before we start counting PPAVs, we first show that a generic isogeny class does contain PPAVs. The question of whether an isogeny class contains PPAVs is answered in [17], but the full condition is complicated. Here, we state the relevant part for our use.

#### Proposition 2.15 ([17, Corollary 11.4]).

An isogeny class of simple ordinary abelian varieties of dimension $g$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ contains a PPAV if $g$ is odd or $K/K^{+}$ is ramified at some finite prime.

The latter condition can be interpreted in the following way.

#### Lemma 2.16.

$K/K^{+}$ is ramified at some finite prime if the Galois group $G$ of $f_{A}(x)$ is not contained in the alternating group $A_{2g}$ .

#### Proof.

We prove the contrapositive. If $K/K^{+}$ is unramified, then the relative discriminant $\Delta_{K/K^{+}}$ is the unit ideal. We can relate the absolute and relative discriminants by $\Delta_{K}=N_{K^{+}/\mathbb{Q}}(\Delta_{K/K^{+}})\Delta_{K^{+}}^{2}$ , so the absolute discriminant $\Delta_{K}$ must be a square. Furthermore, $\disc(f)=\Delta_{K}[\mathcal{O}_{K}\colon\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]^{2}$ where $\alpha$ is a root of $f_{A}(x)$ , so $\disc(f)$ must be a square as well. By [8, Theorem 4.7], this implies that $G$ is contained in $A_{2g}$ . ∎

It follows that an isogeny class of simple ordinary abelian varieties has a PPAV when $G\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ . By Proposition 2.14, this is true generically – there are at most $O(p^{-1/4}\log p)$ proportion of simple ordinary abelian varieties that do not contain a PPAV.

## 3. PPAV counts for a generic characteristic polynomial

There has been much historical work done on counting $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -points over moduli spaces, with the most classical case of modular curves due to Deligne-Rapoport. On a much larger scale, the Langlands-Rapoport conjecture predicts a general formula for the $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ -points over a general Shimura variety. Although this has not yet been proven in general, it is known for many families of Shimura varieties. This includes the family of Siegel Shimura varieties $\mathcal{A}_{g}$ which happens to be one of the simplest examples of Shimura varieties, which Kottwitz detailed in [23, Part III]. We take this as our starting point for this section.

### 3.1. Kottwitz’s orbital integral formula

Let $R$ be a ring. First, we define the notion of an $R$ -isogeny of both abelian varieties and polarized abelian varieties.

#### Definition 3.1.

Let $A$ and $A^{\prime}$ be abelian varieties over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . An $R$ -isogeny of abelian varieties from $A$ to $A^{\prime}$ is an element $\phi\in\Hom_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(A,A^{\prime})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}R$ that is invertible, i.e. there exists an inverse $\psi\in\Hom_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(A^{\prime},A)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}R$ so that $\phi\circ\psi$ and $\psi\circ\phi$ are both the identity in $\End_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(A^{\prime},A^{\prime})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}R$ and $\End_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(A,A)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}R$ respectively. Let $[A,\lambda],[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]$ be polarized abelian varieties. An $R$ -isogeny of polarized abelian varieties is an $R$ -isogeny of abelian varieties $\phi\colon A\rightarrow A^{\prime}$ where $\phi^{*}\lambda\coloneqq\phi^{\vee}\circ\lambda^{\prime}\circ\phi=c\lambda\in\Hom_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(A,A^{\prime})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}R$ for some scalar $c\in R^{\times}$ .

We call a $\mathbb{Q}$ -isogeny of abelian varieties an AV-isogeny, and a $\mathbb{Q}$ -isogeny of polarized abelian varieties a PAV-isogeny, omitting AV or PAV when the context is clear. Also note that two abelian varieties are isogenous in the usual sense if there is a $\mathbb{Q}$ -isogeny between them. Two polarized abelian varieties may not be PAV-isogenous, but may have underlying abelian varieties that are AV-isogenous.

Now, fix a polarized abelian variety $[A,\lambda]$ . We wish to give a formula for the number of PPAVs $[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]$ that are PAV-isogenous to it. Note that here $[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]$ is principally polarized while $[A,\lambda]$ may not be. For $l\neq p$ , consider the action of $\Frob_{p}$ on $H^{1}(A_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_{p}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ which is canonically isomorphic to the dual of $V_{l}=T_{l}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{l}}\mathbb{Q}_{l}$ and hence is a $\mathbb{Q}_{l}$ module of rank $2g$ . By choosing an isomorphism from $H^{1}(A_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_{p}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ to $\mathbb{Q}_{l}^{2g}$ which transports the Weil pairing induced by $\lambda$ to the standard symplectic form, the action of $\Frob_{p}$ gives a $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ up to conjugacy. Simultaneously considering all primes $l\neq p$ gives us $\gamma_{[A,\lambda]}^{p}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{A}_{f}^{p})$ .

For $l=p$ , we consider instead $H^{1}_{cris}(A,\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ whose dual is canonically isomorphic to $D_{0}(A)=D(A)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ . Here, $D(A)$ is the Dieudonné module over the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{p}[F,V]$ , it is free over $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ with rank $2g$ and is equipped with a symplectic form. Then, the Frobenius action $F$ defines an element $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],p}$ of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ with multiplier $p$ up to conjugacy. As a side note, the description in the $l=p$ case is more complicated over the setting of finite fields $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ compared to our case of prime fields $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , for example, one would need to consider twisted conjugacy instead of regular conjugacy.

By considering lattices in the first cohomology groups of PPAVs, Kottwitz proved the following orbital integral formula, which we have simplified slightly in the setting of prime fields $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ .

#### Theorem 3.2 ([23, 205]).

Let $I_{[A,\lambda]}$ be the set of all PPAVs that are isogenous to $[A,\lambda]$ . Then, its groupoid cardinality is

$$ \#I_{[A,\lambda]}=\int_{T_{[A,\lambda]}(\mathbb{Q})\backslash G(\mathbb{A}_{f})}\mathbbm{1}_{G(\hat{\mathbb{Z}}_{f}^{p})}(g^{-1}\gamma^{p}_{[A,\lambda]}g)\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})aG(\mathbb{Z}_{p})}(g^{-1}\gamma_{[A,\lambda],p}g)\ dg $$

where $G=\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ and $a=\diag(p,\ldots,p,1,\ldots,1)$ .

Here, we define the functor $T_{[A,\lambda]}(R)\coloneqq\{\alpha\in(\End_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(A)\otimes R)^{\times}\mid\alpha\alpha^{\dagger}\in R^{\times}\}$ to be the group of $R$ -isogenies from $[A,\lambda]$ to itself. Here, $\alpha^{\dagger}$ is the Rosati involution, which we recall is given by complex conjugation on the CM-field $K$ . From this, it is easy to see that $T_{[A,\lambda]}$ is an algebraic torus over $\mathbb{Q}$ as

$$ T_{[A,\lambda]}=\ker(\mathbb{G}_{m}\times R_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_{m})\rightarrow R_{K^{+}/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_{m})) $$

where $R_{K/L}$ is the restriction of scalars functor and the map sends $(x,y)\mapsto x^{-1}N_{K/K^{+}}(y)$ .

In the case when $[A,\lambda]$ is not principally polarized, it is possible that the orbital integral could evaluate to zero if there are no PPAVs in its PAV-isogeny class. On the other hand, when $[A,\lambda]$ is principally polarized, the orbital integral must be positive. Another way to see this is as follows. Note that $\Frob_{p}$ acts on $H^{1}(A_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_{p}},\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ , and because $\lambda$ is a principal polarization we can choose the isomorphism from $H^{1}(A_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_{p}},\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ to $\mathbb{Q}_{l}^{2g}$ to send $H^{1}(A_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_{p}},\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ to $\mathbb{Z}_{l}^{2g}$ . Hence, we can pick a representative $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ , and by simultaneously considering all primes $l\neq p$ can choose a representative $\gamma_{[A,\lambda]}^{p}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\hat{\mathbb{Z}}_{f}^{p})$ . Similarly, at the prime $p$ , using Dieudonné modules we can choose a representative $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],p}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})a\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{p})$ , so the orbital integral formula is positive.

### 3.2. Reinterpretation as an Euler product

It is difficult to use Kottwitz’s orbital integral formula directly for counting. In [1], Achter-Altuğ-Garcia-Gordon reinterpreted this as a much more concrete Euler product, which we state in the theorem below. However, there is an error in the paper which leads to one of the definitions of $v_{l}([A,\lambda])$ being incorrect. We take care to work around this problem, and this is explained more in Remark 3.4 and the Appendix.

#### Theorem 3.3 ([1, Theorem A]).

Suppose that $[A,\lambda]$ is a PPAV over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ with commutative endomorphism ring (for example, this holds if $A$ is a simple and ordinary). Then,

$$ \#I_{[A,\lambda]}=p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}\tau_{T}v_{\infty}([A,\lambda])\prod_{l}v_{l}([A,\lambda]). $$

We will use this in the case when $A$ is simple and ordinary. We explain the factors appearing in Theorem 3.3. Then, $\tau_{T}$ is the Tamagawa number associated to the algebraic torus $T_{[A,\lambda]}$ . By [31], we can compute this via the formula

$$ \tau_{T}=\frac{|H^{1}(\mathbb{Q},X^{*}(T_{[A,\lambda]})|}{|\Sha^{1}(T_{[A,\lambda]})|} $$

where $\Sha^{1}(T_{[A,\lambda]})=\ker(H^{1}(\mathbb{Q},T)\rightarrow\prod_{v}H^{i}(\mathbb{Q}_{v},T))$ where the product is over all places of $\mathbb{Q}$ , and $X^{*}(T_{[A,\lambda]})$ is the character lattice of $T_{[A,\lambda]}$ .

The local factor at the archimedean place $\infty$ is

$$ v_{\infty}([A,\lambda])=v_{\infty}(f_{A})=\frac{\sqrt{|D(f_{A})|}}{(2\pi)^{g}} $$

where the Weyl discriminant $D(f_{A})\coloneqq\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq g}(2\cos(\theta_{i})-2\cos(\theta_{j}))^{2}\prod_{1\leq i\leq g}4\sin^{2}(\theta_{j})$ where $\sqrt{p}e^{i\theta_{1}},\sqrt{p}e^{-i\theta_{1}},\ldots\sqrt{p}e^{i\theta_{g}},\sqrt{p}e^{-i\theta_{g}}$ are the roots of $f_{A}(x)$ . Another expression for the Weyl discriminant is $D(f_{A})=(-1)^{g}p^{-g(3g-1)/2}\disc(f_{A})/\disc(f^{+}_{A})$ , see Section 6A of loc. cit. [1].

The problem in the paper arises in the non-archimedean local places $v_{l}([A,\lambda])$ , as we explain here.

#### Remark 3.4.

Combining Definition 4.1 and Corollary 3.4 in loc. cit., the incorrect local factor at the non-archimedean place $l$ was written explicitly as

$$ v_{l}([A,\lambda])=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\pi_{k}\left(\Mat_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})\cap\prescript{\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})}{}{\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}}\right)}{\#\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l}/l^{k})/(l^{kg}\psi(l^{k}))} $$

where $\prescript{\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})}{}{\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}}$ is the conjugacy class of $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}$ in $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ , and $\pi_{k}\colon M_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})\rightarrow M_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ is the projection to $\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ . Note that when $l\neq p$ , we can replace $\Mat_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ with $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ because the conjugacy class lies in $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ as the multiplier is coprime to the characteristic.

We give a counterexample in which case this local factor is incorrect. Take $g=1$ , so $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}=\operatorname{GL}_{2}$ . Note that in this particular case, two semisimple elements are conjugate in $\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ if and only if they have the same characteristic polynomial. Picking the characteristic polynomial $x^{2}+5x+4$ and $l=3$ , the incorrect local factor above is

$$ \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\pi_{k}\left(\{\gamma\in GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z}_{3})\mid\tr(\gamma)=5,\det(\gamma)=4\}\right)}{3^{2k-2}(3^{2}-1)} $$

On the other hand, following [16, Equation (3.7)], the correct local factor is given by

$$ \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\left\{\gamma\in GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z}/3^{k}\mathbb{Z})\mid\tr(\gamma)=5,\det(\gamma)=4\right\}}{3^{2k-2}(3^{2}-1)}. $$

The difference is that the first counts projections from $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$ to $\mathbb{Z}/3^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ , while the second directly counts matrices in $\mathbb{Z}/3^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ . It turns out that in this case (more specifically when $l$ divides the discriminant), not every matrix in $\mathbb{Z}/3^{k}\mathbb{Z}$ can be lifted to $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$ such that the characteristic polynomial remains the same. Indeed, running some simple code we see that the first local factor is $7/6$ while the second is $3/2$ . Furthermore, in the $\operatorname{GL}_{2}$ case, the PAV-isogeny class is the same as the AV-isogeny class (see discussion in Section 3.4), so the formula in Theorem 3.3 should yield the same count as [16, Corollary 5.4], but we find that this is not the case.

We pinpoint the problem to the proof of Lemma 3.2 in loc. cit., more specifically the part which uses Hensel’s lemma. The counterexample above can be modified to a counterexample of Lemma 3.2. Fortunately, this mistake is not fatal to our application, as what we need are stable orbital integrals ( $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ conjugacy classes) instead of rational orbital integrals ( $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ conjugacy classes). Gordon and Achter have kindly written an appendix elaborating on this remark, as well as explaining how stable orbital integrals can be written explicitly in terms of Gekeler-style ratios following [16] which we require later.

Even though the explicit formulation of $v_{l}([A,\lambda])$ is incorrect, the arguments relating the orbital integral to the geometric measure is still correct, see Section 5 of loc. cit.. Thus, the product formula in Theorem 3.3 is correct if we use the following definitions of the local factors in Section 5C of loc. cit.:

$$ \begin{split}v_{l}([A,\lambda])&=\frac{l^{\dim(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{F}_{l})}\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}}(\mathbbm{1}_{\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})})\text{ for }l\neq p,\\
v_{p}([A,\lambda])&=p^{-g(g+1)/2}\frac{p^{\dim(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g})}}{\#\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma_{[A,\lambda],p}}(\mathbbm{1}_{G(\mathbb{Z}_{p})aG(\mathbb{Z}_{p})}),\end{split} $$

where the rational orbital integral $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{geom}}_{\gamma}$ is defined at the end of Section 2E of loc. cit.. This definition is rather technical, and we will only use it in the proof of Lemma 3.6. Note that either definition is completely defined by the $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ conjugacy class of $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}$ , so we define $v_{l}(\gamma)$ (including for $l=p$ ) by replacing $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}$ with $\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ in the definitions above so that $v_{l}([A,\lambda])=v_{l}(\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l})$ .

Here, we take the opportunity to define and clarify all the local factors that we use in this paper. We just defined the two archimedean local factors in Equation (3.2). The archimedean local factor associated to trace is $\operatorname{ST}_{g}$ as defined in the introduction.

We have three types of non-archimedean local factors, $v_{l}(t)$ , $v_{l}(f)$ and $v_{l}([A,\lambda])$ , associated to the $p$ -adic density of matrices with a particular trace, characteristic polynomial and PAV-isogeny class respectively, and $v_{l}([A,\lambda])$ was defined in Equation (3.3). For $v_{l}(f)$ , let $M^{*}\subseteq\Mat_{2g}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}$ be the closed scheme cut out by the symplectic equation $A\Omega A^{T}=m\Omega$ where $\Omega=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{g}\\ -I_{g}&0\end{pmatrix}$ , and $M$ be the open subscheme of $M^{*}$ for which the multiplier $m\neq 0$ . Over $\mathbb{Z}_{l}$ , we have $M(\mathbb{Z}_{l})=\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})\cap\Mat_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}_{l})$ . For each prime $l$ (including $l=p$ ), we define

$$ \begin{split}v_{l}(f)&=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\{\gamma\in M(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\mid f_{\gamma}\equiv f\}}{\#\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})/(l^{gk}\phi(l^{k}))}.\end{split} $$

Once again, when $l\neq p$ we can replace $M$ with $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ . We defined $v_{l}(t)$ in the introduction, here we remark on the comment of $v_{p}(t)=1$ .

#### Remark 3.5.

Based on Equation (3.4), morally we should define

$$ v_{l}(t)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\#\{\gamma\in M(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\mid\tr(\gamma)=t,\mult(\gamma)=p\}}{\#\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})/(l^{k}\phi(l^{k}))}. $$

This agrees with our definition for $l\neq p$ , but for $l=p$ we do not do this and instead defined $v_{p}(t)=1$ . The second reason is that because the locally closed subscheme $M$ is much more complicated than $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ , we are unable to prove bounds on the ratio given above, although we expect it to be $1+O(p^{-2})$ like in Proposition 4.4.

The following lemma relates $v_{l}([A,\lambda])$ to $v_{l}(f)$ , and this essentially uses the fact that stable orbital integrals are the disjoint union of rational orbital integrals.

#### Lemma 3.6.

Suppose $\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ is regular semisimple, then we have $v_{l}(f_{\gamma})=\sum_{\gamma^{\prime}}v_{l}(\gamma^{\prime})$ (including $l=p$ ) where the sum is over representatives $\gamma^{\prime}$ of all $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ -conjugacy classes with characteristic polynomial $f_{\gamma^{\prime}}=f_{\gamma}$ .

#### Proof.

### 3.3. Conjugacy classes in reductive groups

We record some facts on conjugacy classes in reductive groups, which we will need later in the case of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ . Let $G$ be a reductive group over a field $k$ , and let $T$ be a maximal torus of $G$ . The Weyl group $W=N(T)/T$ acts on $T$ , and let $T/W\coloneqq\Spec(k[T]^{W})$ .

#### Proposition 3.7.

There exists a map

$$ \chi_{k}\colon\{\text{semisimple conjugacy classes of }G(k)\}\rightarrow(T/W)(k) $$

with the following properties.

- (1) (Steinberg [37]) If $k=\bar{k}$ , then $\chi_{k}$ is bijective.

- (2) (Kottwitz [21]) If $G$ is a quasi-split group with $G^{der}$ simply connected, then $\chi_{k}$ is surjective.

On the issue of injectivity, suppose that $\gamma_{0},\gamma\in G(k)$ are semisimple elements where $\chi_{k}(\gamma_{0})=\chi_{k}(\gamma)$ , which is equivalent to saying that $\gamma_{0},\gamma$ are conjugate in $G(\bar{k})$ . Then, there exists $g\in G(\bar{k})$ such that $g\gamma_{0}g^{-1}=\gamma$ , so for every $\sigma\in\Gal(\bar{k}/k)$ we have $\sigma(g)\gamma_{0}\sigma(g)^{-1}=\gamma$ and thus $g^{-1}\sigma(g)\in G_{\gamma_{0}}(\bar{k})$ . This defines a 1-cocycle $\sigma\mapsto g^{-1}\sigma(g)$ , which gives a class ${}^{-1}(\gamma_{0},\gamma)\in H^{1}(k,G_{\gamma_{0}})$ which is trivial in $H^{1}(k,G)$ . The following proposition shows this class characterizes the semisimple conjugacy class.

#### Proposition 3.8.

(Kottwitz [21]) Suppose $G^{der}$ is simply connected and $\gamma_{0}\in G(k)$ is semisimple. Then, the map $\gamma\mapsto^{-1}(\gamma_{0},\gamma)$ gives a bijection from the set of semisimple conjugacy classes of $G(k)$ which are $G(\bar{k})$ conjugate to $\gamma_{0}$ (i.e. $\chi_{k}^{-1}(\chi_{k}(\gamma_{0}))$ ) to $\ker(H^{1}(k,G_{\gamma_{0}})\rightarrow H^{1}(k,G))$ .

Now, we specialize to the case of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ , a connected, split (hence quasi-split), reductive group. It has derived group $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}$ which is simply connected. Thus, the conditions in both Proposition 3.7 and 3.8 hold. It is easy to see that in our case, $(T/W)(k)$ is in bijection with the monic symplectic polynomials $f(t)\in k[t]$ of degree $2g$ with some multiplier $c\in k^{\times}$ , and correspondingly $\chi_{k}$ sends a matrix to its characteristic polynomial. Hence, by applying part (b) of Proposition 3.7 for $k=\mathbb{Q}$ and part (a) for $k=\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ , we get the following.

#### Corollary 3.9.

Let $f(x)$ be an ordinary Weil $p$ -polynomial. Then, there is a semisimple element $\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q})$ which has characteristic polynomial $f(x)$ which is unique up to $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})$ conjugacy.

We define $\gamma_{A}$ to be a representative of the conjugacy class corresponding to $f_{A}(x)$ .

### 3.4. Kottwitz triples and invariants

By Theorem 3.2 and 3.3, we know the number of PPAVs in a PAV-isogeny class. However, because of the parametrization in Section 2, we would like to know the number of PPAVs in an AV-isogeny class (i.e. those that have some characteristic polynomial). The notion of Kottwitz triples allows us to bridge between these notions. Note that for our setting of prime fields $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , the place $p$ behaves very similarly to places $l\neq p$ , but this is not true for finite fields $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , which requires the notion of twisted conjugacy. Since we are only dealing with prime fields, we ignore twisted conjugacy and simplify all definitions for the specific case of prime fields.

#### Definition 3.10 ([23, 206-207]).

A Kottwitz triple $(\gamma_{0},\gamma,\delta)$ is a triple of elements where

- (1) $\gamma_{0}\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q})$ is a semisimple element defined up to $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})$ conjugacy, where $\gamma_{0}=\gamma_{A}$ for some $g$ -dimensional abelian variety $A$ ,

- (2) $\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{A}^{p}_{f})$ up to $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{A}^{p}_{f})$ conjugacy, such that for every $l\neq p$ , the $l$ -component $\gamma_{l}$ is conjugate to $\gamma_{0}$ in $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ ,

- (3) $\delta\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{p})$ up to conjugacy, where $\delta$ is conjugate to $\gamma_{0}$ in $G(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_{p})$ .

As we saw previously, from a PAV-isogeny class $[A,\lambda]$ we can get the elements $\gamma_{A},\gamma_{[A,\lambda]}^{p}$ and $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],p}$ , one can check these satisfy the conditions required for a Kottwitz triple because they share the same characteristic polynomial. Hence, we get a map

$$ \Phi\colon\{\text{PAV-isogeny classes}\}\rightarrow\{\text{Kottwitz triples}\}. $$

We restrict our attention to a fixed AV-isogeny class of ordinary abelian varieties (i.e. fixed characteristic polynomial), and let $[A,\lambda]$ be a polarized abelian variety such that $A$ is in this isogeny class. Restricting the map $\Phi$ to this AV-isogeny class in turn restricts the Kottwitz triples to those satisfying $\gamma_{0}=\gamma_{A}$ , which gives the following

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Phi_{A}\colon\{\text{PAV-isogeny classes with char poly }f_{A}\}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\{\text{Kottwitz triples }(\gamma_{A},\gamma,\delta)\}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\ker(H^{1}(\mathbb{Q},T_{[A,\lambda]})\rightarrow H^{1}(\mathbb{R},T_{[A,\lambda]}))}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\prod_{l}H^{1}(\mathbb{Q}_{l},T_{[A,\lambda]})}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong} $$

where the bottom arrow is the natural map. From this diagram, we see that every non-empty preimage has cardinality $|\Sha^{1}(T_{[A,\lambda]})|$ , see also [23, 207].

We explain the vertical maps on both sides. On the left, Kottwitz showed that $[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]$ is $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ -isogenous to $[A,\lambda]$ if and only if the underlying abelian varieties $A$ and $A^{\prime}$ are $\mathbb{Q}$ -isogenous, and that the set of $\mathbb{Q}$ -isogeny classes of $[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]$ which are $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ isogenous to $[A,\lambda]$ is in canonical bijection with $\ker(H^{1}(\mathbb{Q},T_{[A,\lambda]})\rightarrow H^{1}(\mathbb{R},T_{[A,\lambda]}))$ [23, 205-206]. On the right, by Proposition 3.8, for each $l\neq p$ , the possible choices of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Q}_{l})$ conjugacy classes for the $l$ -component $\gamma_{l}$ which is $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}_{l})$ conjugate to $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}$ is in canonical bijection to $\ker(H^{1}(\mathbb{Q}_{l},T_{[A,\lambda]})\rightarrow H^{1}(\mathbb{Q}_{l},\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}))\subseteq H^{1}(\mathbb{Q}_{l},T_{[A,\lambda]})$ . Here, we note that by Tate’s theorem [39], $T_{[A,\lambda]}$ is isomorphic to the centralizer of $\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}$ . The same applies to $\delta$ over the prime $p$ .

To describe the image of $\Phi_{A}$ , Kottwitz defined an invariant $\alpha(\gamma_{A},\gamma,\delta)\in\mathfrak{K}(T_{[A,\lambda]})^{D}$ which vanishes if and only if the triple $(\gamma_{A},\gamma,\delta)$ is in the image of $\Phi_{A}$ [23, Theorem 12.1]. Here, $D$ denotes the Pontryagin dual. We omit the construction of this invariant and refer the reader to [23, 166-168]. The only fact we will need from this construction is that $\mathfrak{K}(T_{[A,\lambda]})$ is a subgroup of $\pi_{0}((Z(\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]})/Z(\hat{\operatorname{GSp}}_{2g}))^{\Gamma})$ , where $\Gamma=\Gal(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ is the $L$ -action on the dual groups.

We prove the following proposition, which is absolutely crucial for our proof.

#### Proposition 3.11.

Suppose that $A$ is a simple, ordinary abelian variety whose Galois group is the generic group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ . Then, the group $\pi_{0}((Z(\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]})/Z(\hat{\operatorname{GSp}}_{2g}))^{\Gamma})$ is trivial, so all the invariants $\alpha(\gamma_{A},\gamma,\delta)$ are also trivial and $\Phi_{A}$ is surjective.

#### Proof.

The key ingredient required is the large Galois group, which forces the group of invariants to be small. Recall that $T_{[A,\lambda]}=\ker(\mathbb{G}_{m}\times R_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_{m})\rightarrow R_{K^{+}/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{G}_{m}))$ is a maximal torus in $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ . Over the algebraic closure, we have $T_{[A,\lambda]}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})=\ker\left(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}\times(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times})^{2g}\rightarrow(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times})^{g}\right)$ , where the $2g$ copies of $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}$ correspond to the embeddings of $K\hookrightarrow\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ , and likewise the $g$ copies correspond to the embeddings of $K^{+}\hookrightarrow\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Index the $2g$ copies of $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}$ such that every two consecutive copies correspond to complex conjugate embeddings. One can check that the map above sends $(a,b_{i})_{i\in[2g]}\mapsto(a^{-1}b_{2j-1}b_{2j})_{j\in[g]}$ , and that the Galois action is given by first acting on the scalars in each entry, and then permuting the entries corresponding to the Galois action on the embeddings.

Let $\sigma\in\Gal(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ act on the $2g$ embeddings by the permutation $(1\ 2)^{\epsilon_{1}}\cdots(2g-1\ 2g)^{\epsilon_{g}}f(\rho)$ for some $\epsilon_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ and $\rho\in S_{g}$ , where $f(\rho)$ sends the elements $2i-1$ and $2i$ to $2\rho(i)-1$ and $2\rho(i)$ . The cocharacter lattice $X_{*}(T_{[A,\lambda]})$ has elements $t\mapsto(t^{n},t^{m_{1}},t^{-n-m_{1}},\cdots t^{m_{g}},t^{-n-m_{g}})$ , so it is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^{g+1}$ with coordinates $(n,m_{1},\ldots,m_{g})$ . Then, $\sigma$ sends $(n,m_{1},\ldots,m_{g})\mapsto(n,m_{1}^{\sigma},\ldots,m_{g}^{\sigma})$ where $m_{i}^{\sigma}=m_{\rho^{-1}(i)}$ if $\epsilon_{i}=0$ and $m_{i}^{\sigma}=n-m_{\rho^{-1}(i)}$ if $\epsilon_{i}=1$ .

Using this, we obtain the dual group $\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})=\Hom(X_{*}(T_{[A,\lambda]}),\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times})$ , whose elements are given by $(n,m_{1},\ldots,m_{g})\mapsto a^{n}b_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots b_{g}^{m_{g}}$ . The $L$ -action by $\sigma$ is given by precomposition, so we get $(n,m_{1},\ldots,m_{g})\mapsto(n,m_{1}^{\sigma},\ldots,m_{g}^{\sigma})\mapsto a^{n}b_{1}^{m_{1}^{\sigma}}\cdots b_{g}^{m_{g}^{\sigma}}=(ab_{1}^{\epsilon_{1}}\cdots b_{g}^{\epsilon_{g}})^{n}(b_{\rho(1)}^{(-1)^{\epsilon_{\rho(1)}}})^{m_{1}}\cdots(b_{\rho(g)}^{(-1)^{\epsilon_{\rho(g)}}})^{m_{g}}$ . Hence, $\sigma$ acts on $\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}})\cong(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times})^{g+1}$ by sending $a\mapsto ab_{1}^{\epsilon_{1}}\cdots b_{g}^{\epsilon_{g}}$ and $b_{i}\mapsto b_{\rho(i)}^{(-1)^{\epsilon_{\rho(i)}}}$ .

Let us first find the $\Gamma$ -fixed points of $\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]}$ . Because $A$ has generic Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ , for any choice of $\epsilon_{i},\rho$ there will exist some $\sigma\in\Gal(\bar{\mathbb{Q}},\mathbb{Q})$ acting by the corresponding permutation on the embeddings. By picking $\epsilon_{i}=0$ and $\rho$ to be a cyclic permutation, we get $b_{1}=\cdots=b_{g}$ . Then, by picking $\epsilon_{1}=1$ , $\epsilon_{2}=\cdots=\epsilon_{g}=0$ and $\rho=\id$ , we have $b_{1}=1$ . Hence, the fixed points $\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]}^{\Gamma}$ are $\{(a,1,\ldots,1)\mid a\in\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}\}$ . Note that $Z(\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]})=\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]}$ because $\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]}$ is a torus.

Lastly, $Z(\hat{\operatorname{GSp}}_{2g})=Z(\text{GSpin}_{2g+1})$ is one-dimensional and lies inside $Z(\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]})$ as $\{(a,1,\ldots,1)\mid a\in\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}\}$ , so we have that $\pi_{0}((Z(\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]})/Z(\hat{\operatorname{GSp}}_{2g}))^{\Gamma})$ is trivial. ∎

We remark that similar computations were done in [34] and [1, Appendix], although not in the setting of the generic Galois group. One could also loosen the condition on the Galois group. More importantly, this computation also shows us that the numerator in the Tamagawa number is $1$ .

#### Corollary 3.12.

Suppose that $A$ is a simple, ordinary abelian variety with generic Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{g}\rtimes S_{g}$ . Then, $H^{1}(\mathbb{Q},X^{*}(T_{[A,\lambda]}))$ is trivial.

#### Proof.

Kottwitz’s isomorphism gives $H^{1}(\mathbb{Q},X^{*}(T_{[A,\lambda]}))\cong\pi_{0}(Z(\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]})^{\Gamma})$ [22, Equation (2.4.1), Section 2.4.3], and by the proof of Proposition 3.11 we have that $Z(\hat{T}_{[A,\lambda]})^{\Gamma}=\{(a,1,\ldots,1)\mid a\in\bar{\mathbb{Q}}^{\times}\}$ is connected. ∎

### 3.5. Proof of Theorem 1.10

We end this section by proving the theorem on PPAV counts for a characteristic polynomial. The fact that there are a nonzero number of PPAVs follows from the generic Galois group, Proposition 2.15 and Lemma 2.16. Let $[A,\lambda]$ be a polarization of $A$ . By Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.12,

$$ \#I_{[A,\lambda]}=\frac{p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}}{|\Sha^{1}(T_{[A,\lambda]})|}v_{\infty}(f_{A})\prod_{l}v_{l}(\gamma_{[A,\lambda],l}). $$

We wish to sum up all $\#I_{[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]}$ over all PAV-isogeny classes $[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]$ which have characteristic polynomial $f_{A}$ . By Proposition 3.11, the map

$$ \Phi_{A}\colon\{\text{PAV-isogeny classes with char poly }f_{A}\}\rightarrow\{\text{Kottwitz triples }(\gamma_{A},\gamma,\delta)\} $$

is surjective and $|\Sha^{1}(T_{[A,\lambda]})|$ -to- $1$ . Hence, applying Lemma 3.6 we have

$$ \begin{split}\sum_{[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]}\#I_{[A^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}]}&=|\Sha^{1}(T_{[A,\lambda]})|\sum_{(\gamma_{l})}\frac{p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}}{|\Sha^{1}(T_{[A,\lambda]})|}v_{\infty}(f_{A})\prod_{l}v_{l}(\gamma_{l})\\
&=p^{\dim(\mathcal{A}_{g})/2}v_{\infty}(f_{A})\prod_{l}v_{l}(f_{A})\end{split} $$

as desired. Here, the tuple $(\gamma_{l})$ includes the place $p$ where $\gamma_{p}=\delta$ , and the products over $l$ include $p$ too. One could worry about commuting infinite products and sums, but this is not a problem here as there are only a finite number of PAV-isogeny classes which contribute a nonzero count.

## 4. Properties of local factors

In this section we prove some technical lemmas about the local factors $v_{\infty}(f)$ , $v_{l}(f)$ and $v_{l}(t)$ , which we will need in the later sections. Let $A$ be a simple ordinary abelian variety with characteristic polynomial $f_{A}$ , which we denote as $f$ for convenience.

### 4.1. $v_{\infty}(f)$

Recall that we defined the Steinberg map $\pi\colon\operatorname{USp}_{2g}\rightarrow\mathcal{R}_{g}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{g}$ to send a matrix to the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial in Lemma 2.6. Let $\mu_{\mathcal{R}_{g}}=\pi_{*}\mu_{\operatorname{USp}_{2g}}$ be the pushforward of the Haar measure on $\operatorname{USp}_{2g}$ . Note that the trace map $\tr\colon\operatorname{USp}_{2g}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is obtained by projecting on the first entry $p_{1}\circ\pi$ , so we can write the Sato-Tate measure as $\mu_{\operatorname{ST}_{g}}=(p_{1})_{*}\mu_{\mathcal{R}_{g}}$ . The following proposition gives an important interpretation of archimedean local factor $v_{\infty}(f)=\sqrt{|D(f)|}/(2\pi)^{g}$ as the density function of the measure $\mu_{\mathcal{R}_{g}}$ , hence relating it to the Sato-Tate measure.

#### Proposition 4.1.

For $\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{R}_{g}$ , we have

$$ \mu_{\mathcal{R}_{g}}=\frac{\sqrt{\left|D\left(f_{[p](\mathbf{b})}\right)\right|}}{(2\pi)^{g}}db_{1}\cdots db_{g}, $$

where $f_{[p](\mathbf{b})}=x^{2g}+b_{1}p^{1/2}x^{2g-1}+\cdots+p^{g}$ was defined in Definition 2.4.

#### Proof.

By the Weyl integration formula [20, Section 5.0.4], the Haar measure of the part of $\operatorname{USp}_{2g}$ that corresponds to the angles being inside $(\theta_{1},\theta_{1}+d\theta_{1}),\ldots,(\theta_{g},\theta_{g}+d\theta_{g})$ up to permutation is $\prod_{i}(\frac{2}{\pi}\sin^{2}(\theta_{i}))\prod_{i<j}(2\cos(\theta_{i})-2\cos(\theta_{j}))^{2}$ . By Lemma 2.6 any element in $\operatorname{USp}_{2g}$ has a characteristic polynomial $g_{\mathbf{b}}(x)$ with $\mathbf{b}\in\mathcal{R}_{g}$ with roots $e^{\pm i\theta_{1}},\ldots,e^{\pm i\theta_{g}}$ , so when we translate the Haar measure to the coefficients $b_{i}$ , we need to divide by $|\det((\frac{db_{j}}{d\theta_{k}})_{j,k})|$ , and it suffices to compute this.

Recall that $g^{+}_{\mathbf{b}}(x)=x^{g}+c_{1}x^{g-1}+\cdots+c_{g}$ has roots $e^{i\theta_{1}}+e^{-i\theta_{1}},\ldots,e^{i\theta_{g}}+e^{-i\theta_{g}}$ , and from the proof of Lemma 2.9 the coefficients $c_{i}$ are given by $b_{i}$ plus a linear combination of $b_{i-2},b_{i-4},\ldots$ , which implies that $\det((\frac{db_{j}}{d\theta_{k}})_{j,k})=\det((\frac{dc_{j}}{d\theta_{k}})_{j,k})$ . Using Vieta’s formulas, we obtain

$$ \frac{dc_{j}}{d\theta_{k}}=\frac{d}{d\theta_{k}}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[g]\\
|S|=j\end{subarray}}\prod_{s\in S}(e^{i\theta_{s}}+e^{-i\theta_{s}})\right)=-\sin(\theta_{k})2^{j}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[g]\setminus\{k\}\\
|S|=j-1\end{subarray}}\prod_{s\in S}\cos(\theta_{s}). $$

After factoring both $-\sin(\theta_{k})$ and $2^{j}$ out of the matrix we have

$$ \det\left(\left(\frac{dc_{j}}{d\theta_{k}}\right)_{j,k}\right)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{g}-2^{i}\sin(\theta_{i})\right)\cdot\det\begin{pmatrix}1&x_{2}+x_{3}+\cdots+x_{g}&\cdots&x_{2}x_{3}\cdots x_{g}\\
1&x_{1}+x_{3}+\cdots+x_{g}&\cdots&x_{1}x_{3}\cdots x_{g}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
1&x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{g-1}&\cdots&x_{1}x_{2}\cdots x_{g-1}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where we write $x_{i}=\cos(\theta_{i})$ . To evaluate the determinant of the matrix on the right, we subtract the first row from the other rows to get

$$ \begin{pmatrix}1&x_{2}+x_{3}+\cdots+x_{g}&\cdots&x_{2}x_{3}\cdots x_{g}\\
0&x_{1}-x_{2}&\cdots&(x_{1}-x_{2})x_{3}\cdots x_{g}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&x_{1}-x_{g}&\cdots&(x_{1}-x_{g})x_{2}\cdots x_{g-1}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Factoring out the $x_{1}-x_{i}$ factor for rows $2\leq i\leq g$ , we realize that the lower right $(g-1)\times(g-1)$ submatrix is of the same form as the first matrix with the variables $x_{2},\ldots,x_{g}$ instead. Using this, we inductively compute the determinant to be $\prod_{i<j}(x_{i}-x_{j})$ . Putting everything together and recalling that $D(f_{[p](\mathbf{b})})=\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq g}(2\cos(\theta_{i})-2\cos(\theta_{j}))^{2}\prod_{1\leq i\leq g}4\sin^{2}(\theta_{j})$ , we have that the density function of $\mu_{\mathcal{R}_{g}}$ is $\frac{\sqrt{|D(f_{[p](\mathbf{b})})|}}{(2\pi)^{g}}$ . ∎

### 4.2. $v_{l}(t)$

Before we look at $v_{l}(f)$ , we first tackle the easier case of $v_{l}(t)$ . Recall that for this paper we assumed $g\geq 2$ , which is a necessary condition for the results here. Since we already defined $v_{p}(t)=1$ , for the rest of this subsection we can restrict our attention to $l\neq p$ , for which $v_{l}(t)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}v_{l,k}(t)$ where we let

$$ v_{l,k}(t)=\frac{\#\{\gamma\in\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})\mid\tr(\gamma)=t,\text{mult}(\gamma)=p\}}{\#\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})/(l^{k}\phi(l^{k}))}. $$

Let $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p,t}$ be the subscheme of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}$ cut out by trace $t$ and multiplier $p$ , so the numerator above is simply $\#\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p,t}(\mathbb{Z}/l^{k}\mathbb{Z})$ . The main goal here is to bound $v_{l}(t)=1+O(l^{-2})$ , and give a quantitative statement about the convergence of $v_{l,k}(t)$ to $v_{l}(t)$ . Later we will see that analogous statements for $v_{l}(f)$ are much harder to prove. This is because in the $v_{l}(t)$ case the singularities of $\operatorname{GSp}_{2g,p,t}$ are more tractable compared to the $v_{l}(f)$ case.
